passage: Sports day rehearsal ran through the lunch break, and the tiffin boxes stayed in the classroom. By the last period Asif Sir noticed that Vaibhav, usually easy-going, was drumming his pencil, losing his place in the reading twice and snapping at his bench-mate, "Move your elbow or I'll move it!" A few children giggled. Asif's first thought was to send him to the back. Then he remembered Vaibhav's tiffin coming back unopened. "Vaibhav, did you get to eat?" Vaibhav shook his head, eyes on the desk. Asif let him eat his parathas quietly at the side table for a few minutes, then carried on with the lesson. The pencil went still.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav say to his bench-mate?
qa.a: "Move your elbow or I'll move it!"

qa.q: What made Asif Sir change his mind about sending Vaibhav to the back?
qa.a: He felt a flash of irritation, then concern when he remembered the unopened tiffin and guessed hunger was behind the snapping.

qa.q: What choice helped here, and why?
qa.a: Letting Vaibhav eat quietly for a few minutes; it met the physical need instead of punishing it as bad behaviour.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt if he had been sent to the back?
qa.a: Embarrassed and unfairly punished for something his hungry body was doing, and still unable to focus.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing an edgy, distracted, quarrelsome child and recognising a missed lunch as the cause instead of punishing him.

passage: In the art room of a Bandra school, Maria Miss watched Bhavna tear up her third drawing of the afternoon. Bhavna, nine, was usually the calm one in her group. Today she argued with Rukhsar over the glue, stared out of the window during the instructions and told Pranav his idea was "stupid". Maria remembered the lunch hall: Bhavna had pushed her dal-rice around and gone out to play after two bites. Instead of a warning, Maria knelt by her desk. "Tummy empty?" Bhavna nodded. Maria gave her a banana from her own bag and a quiet corner, and made a note to mention lunch to Bhavna's parents at pickup. By the bell, Bhavna was helping Rukhsar with the glue.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do with her dal-rice at lunch?
qa.a: She pushed it around and went out to play after two bites.

qa.q: What did Maria suspect when Bhavna tore up her drawing, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She suspected hunger rather than bad behaviour and felt concerned, remembering the barely touched lunch.

qa.q: How could Maria's note to the parents help?
qa.a: It lets the family know Bhavna is barely eating lunch, so together they can find food she will eat and not treat the edginess as bad behaviour.

qa.q: What might the afternoon have felt like for Bhavna before Maria knelt by her?
qa.a: Probably miserable and scratchy; with an empty stomach she could not settle, so she tore up drawings and snapped at her group.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher noticing a child who ate little at lunch turning edgy and quarrelsome, and treating it as hunger rather than misbehaviour.

passage:
"Mohit, that's the third time you've shoved Kabir's bag."
"He keeps moving it into my space!"
"Mm. And you snapped at Sana too. Come here a second."
"What?"
"Did you eat your lunch today?"
"Not really. It was karela. I gave it to the crows."
"And breakfast?"
"Just tea. I was late."
"So you've been running on tea since seven. No wonder everything is annoying."
"I'm not hungry."
"Your stomach just growled at me. I have an extra paratha in my box. Eat it by the window, then come back."
Ten minutes later:
"Kabir, sorry about your bag."
"It's okay."
"Arohi Ma'am, thank you."

qa.q: What did Mohit do with his lunch?
qa.a: He gave it to the crows.

qa.q: What made Arohi suspect hunger rather than naughtiness?
qa.a: Arohi was puzzled by the shoving and snapping and concerned enough to ask about lunch and breakfast before blaming him.

qa.q: What did Arohi's response get right?
qa.a: She treated the edginess as a physical need, fed him, and let him settle before he apologised on his own.

qa.q: How might Kabir see Mohit's shoving?
qa.a: Kabir may have thought Mohit was just being mean, not knowing he had been running on tea since seven.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a child who skipped lunch turning edgy and quarrelsome, and treating the hunger rather than punishing the behaviour.

passage: The first month I taught Class 3, I nearly sent Urmila home with a note for fighting. She was a quiet, careful girl in the mornings, but every afternoon she turned prickly, arguing over pencils, staring out of the window, forgetting what I had just said. One Thursday I watched her at lunch instead of marking copies. She opened her tiffin, looked in, and closed it again. Two dry rotis, and she didn't like them cold. When I asked, she said she'd rather wait for home. Home was at four. So that was the afternoons. I spoke to her mother at pickup, and we agreed on something she liked, poha in a flask. The arguing mostly stopped. I'm Alka, and when a child gets difficult after lunch, I check the tiffin first now.

qa.q: What was in Urmila's tiffin?
qa.a: Two dry rotis.

qa.q: How did Alka feel on realising why Urmila was prickly?
qa.a: Alka felt a mix of relief and some guilt, having nearly sent a note home for fighting when Urmila was simply hungry.

qa.q: What did Alka do that solved the problem?
qa.a: Alka spoke to Urmila's mother and together they chose food she would eat, poha in a flask, instead of punishing her.

qa.q: What were the afternoons like for Urmila?
qa.a: She was hungry until four, which left her edgy and distracted, and probably upset at being in trouble.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a child who ate little at lunch becoming edgy and quarrelsome, and recognising hunger instead of treating it as bad behaviour.

passage:
PE notes, Friday, Class 6B
Sangeeta pushed Anjali during kho-kho today and then argued with me about the rule, red-faced. That's out of character; she's usually my calmest captain. She also couldn't remember which side she was chasing. I asked her to sit in the shade and asked when she'd last eaten. She said she had skipped lunch to finish her art project in the classroom. I gave her the biscuits from the first-aid box and some water, and after ten minutes she went to apologise to Anjali on her own. I've told her class teacher, and we'll make sure the art room stays closed during lunch.
Nikita

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta skip lunch?
qa.a: To finish her art project in the classroom.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she argued about the rule?
qa.a: She was edgy and flustered, red-faced and muddled about the game, because she was running on an empty stomach.

qa.q: What will stop this happening again?
qa.a: Keeping the art room closed at lunch so she eats, and reading hunger as the cause rather than punishing the push.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when Sangeeta came to apologise?
qa.a: Anjali was likely surprised and relieved, since pushing is not like her usual calm captain.

grounding: Shows an adult noticing a child who skipped lunch turning quarrelsome and forgetful, and treating hunger as the cause rather than bad behaviour.

passage:
Tuesday night
Strange afternoon. Alka, my quietest girl in Class 5, pushed Sameer off the bench after lunch and then argued with me about the maths homework, eyes flashing. I was about to send her to the corridor. Then I remembered her lunchbox at recess: two bites, then shut. When I asked, she muttered that she didn't like today's sabzi and wasn't hungry then. By three she clearly was. I gave her the spare biscuits from my drawer and a glass of water, and let her sit by the window. Twenty minutes later she apologised to Sameer on her own. Note to self: check lunchboxes, not just behaviour.
Pallavi

qa.q: What did Pallavi give Alka?
qa.a: The spare biscuits from the drawer and a glass of water.

qa.q: What was Pallavi about to do, and what made her pause?
qa.a: Pallavi felt irritated enough to send Alka to the corridor, then paused on remembering the lunchbox shut after two bites.

qa.q: What lesson did Pallavi take from the afternoon?
qa.a: To check lunchboxes, not just behaviour, since hunger can look like bad behaviour.

qa.q: How might Alka have been feeling by three o'clock?
qa.a: She was probably hungry and edgy, which made her quick to push and argue.

grounding: A teacher notices that a child who ate little at lunch is edgy and quarrelsome and treats the hunger instead of punishing.
